66	Table~\ref{tab:main} compares Plan~A (Section~\ref{sec:adaptive_k_method}) with analysis baselines that isolate the contribution of selection and correction at fixed $K$.
67	
68	\paragraph{Plan~A: selective correction at $K{=}2$.}
69	The proposed pipeline achieves $18.3 \pm 2.1$\% on Object (3 seeds) and $35.0 \pm 1.0$\% on Spatial, exceeding the best fixed-$K$ baseline (CRM $K{=}10$: $16.8$\%, $34.4$\%) with 80\% fewer VLA forward passes ($K{=}2$ vs.\ $K{=}10$). On Object, the 83.7\% CRM trigger rate means 16.3\% of steps use the fast path (argmin-to-centroid only), avoiding over-correction on easy steps. On Spatial, the trigger rate reaches 97.6\%, indicating that CRM correction is almost universally beneficial on this easier benchmark where most steps already fall near the policy mode. This selective application outperforms unconditional correction at $K{=}10$, consistent with the finding that over-triggering degrades performance (P25 $<$ P50, Table~\ref{tab:adaptive}). With only $K{=}2$ samples, the centroid estimate has lower variance than with $K{=}10$, providing a cleaner starting point for the CRM's bounded correction ($\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_2 \leq \varepsilon$).

\paragraph{Component decomposition (fixed-$K$ analysis).}
\looseness=-1 The remaining rows of Table~\ref{tab:main} are analysis baselines at fixed $K$, not proposed methods. CRM obs\_only at $K{=}10$ reaches $16.8 \pm 1.8$\% on Object ($p{=}0.003$) and $34.4 \pm 1.5$\% on Spatial. Random selection fails to exceed VLA-only ($9.7$\% vs.\ $11.0$\%), confirming that sampling without ranking is insufficient; argmin adds $+$1.3\,pp, and CRM correction contributes $+$4.5\,pp (78\% of the gain). At $K{=}5$, correction contributes 55\%. At $K{=}1$, correction without centering falls below baseline ($10.3$\%), validating the $K{\geq}2$ requirement.

\looseness=-1 Three distribution shifts define the pipeline's operating boundaries.
\textbf{(1) Input shift} ($K{=}1$, 10.3\%): without argmin centering, correction direction is unreliable.
\textbf{(2) Task shift}: near-OOD (leave-task-out) is adversarial ($2$\% vs.\ $14$\% VLA-only, $-$12\,pp); far-OOD is neutral (Goal $68.0$\% vs.\ $68.7$\%, $p{=}0.46$) or marginal (Long-horizon $+$2.3\,pp, $p{=}0.061$).
\textbf{(3) Feature shift}: loosening $\varepsilon$ amplifies noisy per-DOF covariance estimates (perdof: ${\sim}$14\% $\to$ 0\%; Section~\ref{sec:magnitude_results}).
All three share a mechanism: CRM degrades when inputs depart from training distribution; all Table~\ref{tab:main} results are in-distribution.

Improvement concentrates on medium-difficulty tasks (Appendix~\ref{sec:per_task}). Under batched inference, Plan~A's $K{=}2$ pipeline runs 1.82$\times$ faster than the $K{=}10$ baseline; CRM adds only 0.28\,ms overhead (Appendix~\ref{sec:latency}).

2	\section{Conclusion}
3	\label{sec:conclusion}
4	
5	\looseness=-2 We presented an adaptive inference-time compute pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. The $K{=}2$ $L_2$ probe ($\rho{=}0.9979$) gates selective CRM correction, achieving $18.3$\% Object / $35.0$\% Spatial ($+$7.3 / $+$5.7\,pp vs.\ VLA-only) while matching or exceeding fixed-$K{=}10$ unconditional correction with 80\% fewer VLA forward passes. On fixed-$K$ analysis baselines, learned correction contributes 55--78\% of the gain. Three distribution shifts define operating boundaries: near-OOD is adversarial ($-$12\,pp), far-OOD neutral ($p{=}0.46$).
6	\textbf{Limitations.}\enspace All experiments use LIBERO in simulation with a single VLA (SmolVLA, 450M). Real-robot transfer and larger flow-matching VLAs (e.g., $\pi_0$) are untested; CRM effectiveness may differ with model capacity. Absolute success rates (18.3\% Object, 35.0\% Spatial) are far from deployment-ready. The CRM requires task-specific calibration and does not generalize to unseen tasks ($-$12\,pp; Section~\ref{sec:failure_modes}). The $K{=}2$ $L_2$ probe is validated only for flow-matching generation; whether analogous cheap uncertainty signals exist for diffusion-based or other stochastic VLA architectures remains open. More broadly, the pipeline requires stochastic sample diversity, excluding tokenized VLAs (Appendix~\ref{sec:applicability}). The threshold $\tau$ may require recalibration for new domains. AI tools assisted with code and manuscript.

Small $\varepsilon$ masks this noise; large $\varepsilon$ amplifies it into compounding drift. obs\_only sidesteps this entirely by conditioning on the observation embedding and global $L_2$ uncertainty, avoiding per-DOF covariance estimation. The limitation is sample efficiency relative to action dimensionality, not CRM architecture. scalar (8.5\%) falls below VLA-only. obs\_only is used throughout.

37	To validate the $K{=}2$ probe as an uncertainty signal independently of Plan~A, we test a variable-$K$ protocol that expands to $K{=}10$ on high-uncertainty steps (details in Appendix~\ref{sec:spatial_adaptive}).

However, Plan~A ($K{=}2$ selective CRM) Pareto-dominates all variable-$K$ thresholds: $18.3$\% at avg\_$K{=}2$, exceeding even fixed $K{=}10$ ($16.8$\%) while using 80\% fewer VLA forward passes. The variable-$K$ sweep confirms that the $K{=}2$ uncertainty signal is effective for adaptive allocation, but its optimal utilization is selective CRM correction rather than expanding the sample budget.

1	Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation degrade under distribution shift, yet improving their outputs at inference time remains underexplored, particularly the question of \emph{when} additional compute is warranted.
2	We propose an adaptive inference-time compute pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. The core mechanism is a $K{=}2$ pairwise $L_2$ distance that correlates near-perfectly with full $K{=}10$ sample variance ($\rho{=}0.9979$), providing a per-step uncertainty estimate at zero additional cost. Three alternative signals (FMVD, CRM correction magnitude) all fail ($\rho \leq 0.15$).
3	When uncertainty is low, the pipeline outputs the $K{=}2$ argmin sample directly; when high, it applies learned residual correction via a ${\sim}$327K-parameter Correction Residual Module (CRM) trained on task-specific VLA rollout data. The pipeline uses at most two forward passes---gains come from learned correction, not additional sampling.
4	The $K{=}2$ adaptive pipeline matches or exceeds fixed-$K{=}10$ unconditional correction with 80\% fewer VLA forward passes: $18.3 \pm 2.1$\% on LIBERO-Object ($+$7.3\,pp vs.\ VLA-only) and $35.0 \pm 1.0$\% on LIBERO-Spatial ($+$5.7\,pp), with selective CRM application (Object 83.7\%, Spatial 97.6\% trigger rate).
5	Component decomposition on fixed-$K$ analysis baselines reveals that learned correction contributes 55\% of the gain at $K{=}5$ and 78\% at $K{=}10$, while multi-sampling is an enabling condition ($K{=}1$ correction degrades below baseline). Three distribution shifts define operating boundaries: near-OOD task shift is adversarial ($-$12\,pp) while far-OOD is neutral.

0	\section{Introduction}
1	\label{sec:intro}
2	
3	Deploying a pretrained Vision-Language-Action model (VLA) on a new task typically requires fine-tuning on task-specific demonstrations, yet collecting such data is expensive and the resulting checkpoint may not generalize further.
4	An alternative is to keep the VLA frozen and attach a lightweight post-hoc correction module trained on task-specific VLA rollout data, improving action quality at inference time without modifying the base model.
5	Flow-matching VLAs~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla,lipman2023flow} are natural candidates: each forward pass produces a stochastic action sample, so drawing multiple samples opens the door to selection and correction without changing model weights.
6	The question is not only how to use these samples but \emph{when} to invest the additional compute: most control steps are easy and do not benefit from multi-sample correction, while a minority of hard steps account for the majority of task failures.
7	
8	Recent robustness evaluations~\cite{fei2025liberoplus} show that state-of-the-art VLAs lose over 65 percentage points under common deployment perturbations, making inference-time correction practically relevant.
9	Training-time methods~\cite{srpo2025,robustvla2025,digflow2025,liu2026ttvla} improve the base policy through robustness-aware objectives or test-time RL, but require retraining and remain bounded by the training distribution.

Unlike DA-SIP, which adapts denoising steps within a diffusion policy, our probe operates in action space and triggers a qualitatively different computation path (selection + learned correction) rather than adjusting iteration count.
Conformal prediction~\cite{angelopoulos2023gentle} has been applied to robotics for safety constraints~\cite{zhou2025acp_cbf,wang2025cploop} and teleoperation calibration~\cite{zhao2024conformalized}; we test CP scores as correction features and find they do not improve over observation-only conditioning (Section~\ref{sec:magnitude_results}).
